p.src: The tale tells how Tripitaka and his disciples arrived at the Chanlin Monastery of Zhenhai, where the monks welcomed them and prepared a vegetarian meal. When the four pilgrims had finished eating, the woman also received some food and regained a little strength. Gradually darkness fell, and lamps were lit in the abbot's quarters. The monks crowded together in rows beneath the lamps, partly to ask the Tang monk about the origins of his scripture-seeking journey, and partly because they were eager to look at the woman. Tripitaka said to the lama monk whom they had first met, “Master of the monastery, once we leave your honored mountain tomorrow, what is the road westward like?” The monk dropped to both knees. The elder hastily caught hold of him and said, “Please rise, Master of the monastery. I merely asked you about the road. Why do you bow to me?” The monk replied, “Venerable master, the road westward tomorrow is level and easy, so you need not worry. It is only that there is an awkward matter before us. I meant to mention it as soon as you entered, but feared offending your august dignity. Only now that the meal is over do I dare report it: you masters have come a long and arduous way from the east, and it would be very well for all of you to rest in this humble monk's quarters; but accommodating this female bodhisattva is inconvenient, and I do not know where we should ask her to sleep.” Tripitaka said, “Master of the monastery, do not become suspicious and imagine that my disciples and I harbor improper intentions. This morning, while passing through the Black Pine Forest, we came upon this woman bound to a tree. My young disciple Sun Wukong refused to rescue her, but I was moved by a bodhisattva's compassion and set her free. Now that we are here, you may send her to sleep wherever you see fit.” The monk thanked him, saying, “Since the venerable master is so generous, let her go to the Hall of the Heavenly Kings. We shall make her a bed of straw behind the Heavenly King and have her sleep there.” Tripitaka said, “Excellent, excellent.” Thereupon the young monks led the woman away to sleep behind the hall. The elder remained in the abbot's quarters, told the monastery masters to make themselves at ease, and they all dispersed. Tripitaka instructed Wukong, “You have worked hard. Let us sleep early and rise early.” They all slept together in one place, not daring to leave their master's side as they kept watch over him. p.src: Of the night's conversation, we shall say no more. When dawn came, the Pilgrim rose and told Bajie and Sha Monk to pack the luggage and ready the horse, then went to ask their master to resume the journey. At that hour the elder was still deep in sleep and had not awakened. The Pilgrim approached and called, “Master.” His master raised his head a little but could not manage an answer. The Pilgrim asked, “Master, what is the matter?” The elder groaned, “Why is my head so dizzy, my eyes so swollen, and all my flesh and bones aching?” Hearing this, Bajie reached out and felt his body; it was somewhat feverish. The idiot laughed and said, “I know what it is. Last night he saw the food cost nothing, ate several bowls too many, then slept with his head in a draught. He has given himself indigestion.” The Pilgrim barked, “Nonsense! Let me ask Master exactly what happened.” Tripitaka said, “In the middle of the night I rose to relieve myself without putting on my cap. I expect the wind chilled me.” The Pilgrim said, “That makes sense. Can you travel now?” Tripitaka replied, “I cannot even sit up now. How could I mount the horse? But this will only delay our journey!” The Pilgrim said, “Master, what are you saying? As the common saying goes, ‘A teacher for one day is a father for life.’ Since we are your disciples, we are just like your sons. Another saying goes, ‘Raising sons requires neither gold nor silver; what matters is that they know what to do when the occasion arises.’ Since you are unwell, why speak of delaying the journey? What harm could there be in patiently resting for a few days?” The brothers all waited upon their master, and before they knew it morning had passed into noon and dusk had fallen; no sooner had the fair night ended than dawn came again.

p.src: Time flew swiftly, and three days had soon passed. That day, the master stirred and sat up, calling, “Wukong, these past two days my illness has weighed heavily upon me, and I have not had a chance to ask you: has anyone taken food to that female bodhisattva who escaped with her life?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Why concern yourself with her? Look after your own illness first.” Tripitaka said, “Quite right, quite right. Help me sit up, then take out my paper, brush, and ink, and borrow an inkstone from the monastery for me.” The Pilgrim asked, “What for?” The elder replied, “I wish to compose a letter and seal it together with our travel rescript. Take them to the imperial court in Chang'an for me and seek an audience with Emperor Taizong.” The Pilgrim said, “That is easy. There are other things in which old Monkey has little ability, but when it comes to delivering letters, I am foremost in the world. Prepare the letter and give it to me. p.src: When the Pilgrim heard this, he could not restrain a hearty laugh. “Master, you are far too fainthearted! At the slightest touch of illness, you begin entertaining such thoughts. If your illness truly worsens and your life hangs in the balance, you need only tell me. Old Monkey has his own way of dealing with it: which King of Hell would dare conceive the thought of taking you? Which judge would dare issue the warrant? Which ghostly constable would come to seize your soul? If they provoke me, I shall let loose the temper with which I once threw Heaven into turmoil, fight my way into the underworld with my cudgel, seize the Ten Kings of Hell, and tear out their sinews one by one—and even then I shall not spare them.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, I am gravely ill. Do not make such extravagant boasts.”

p.src: Bajie stepped forward and said, “Elder Brother, Master says he is in a bad way, yet you insist he is well. That is most inappropriate. We had better make plans while there is still time: first sell the horse and pawn the luggage, then buy a coffin, see him to his end, and cremate him.” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, you are talking nonsense again. You do not understand. Master was the second disciple of the Buddha Tathagata, originally called Elder Golden Cicada. Only because he treated the Dharma with disrespect was he destined to undergo this great tribulation.” Bajie said, “Brother, if Master was banished back to the Eastern Land for disrespecting the Dharma, was incarnated as a man amid the sea of strife and the arena of contention, vowed to journey to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures, and has been bound whenever he met a fiend and hung up whenever he encountered a demon, then surely all the suffering he has endured is enough. Why must he now be made ill as well?” The Pilgrim said, “What would you know about it? Once, while our venerable master was listening to the Buddha preach the Dharma, he dozed off. When he stretched out his foot, his left foot spilled a single grain of rice. For that offense, he was destined to suffer these three days of illness after descending to the mortal world.” Bajie exclaimed in alarm, “Old Pig spills food everywhere whenever he eats. Who knows how many years of illness I must be due!” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, you do not know that the Buddha does not hold such thoughts against ordinary beings. People say, ‘Hoeing grain beneath the noonday sun, sweat falls upon the soil below. Who knows that every grain in the bowl was won by bitter toil?’ Master has only today left to endure; tomorrow he will recover.” Tripitaka said, “Today I feel different from yesterday: my throat is terribly parched. Go and find some cool water somewhere for me to drink.” The Pilgrim said, “You are recovering! If Master wants water to drink, that means you are getting well. Wait here while I fetch some water.”

p.src: He immediately took the alms bowl and went to the monastery kitchen at the rear for water. Suddenly he saw that every monk had red-rimmed eyes and was choking back sobs, though none dared weep aloud. Pilgrim said, “You monks are terribly petty-minded. We shall stay only a few days, and when we leave we will thank you and repay the cost of firewood for every day. Why act like such miserable wretches?” The monks hurriedly knelt and said, “We would not dare! We would not dare!” Pilgrim said, “What would you not dare do? Is it that long-snouted monk of ours has such a vast appetite that he has eaten away your capital?” The monks said, “My lord, though ours is a remote mountain, we have around a hundred monks, great and small. If each supported you for one day, we could maintain you for a hundred days. How could we be so heartless as to begrudge you food and provisions?” Pilgrim said, “If you do not begrudge it, why are you crying?” The monks said, “My lord, some evil monster from the mountains has entered this monastery, though we know not what it is. Each night we send two young monks to strike the bell and beat the drum. Once we hear the bell and drum finish sounding, they never return. When we search the next day, we find only their caps and shoes cast in the rear garden, with their bones still lying there—the men have been eaten. In the three days you have stayed here, six monks have vanished from our monastery. That is why we brothers cannot help being afraid and grieving. Seeing your venerable master ill, we dared not tell you; but we could not keep our tears from secretly falling.” Hearing this, Pilgrim was both startled and delighted. “Say no more. A demon must certainly be harming people here. Let me exterminate it for you.” The monks said, “My lord, no fiend could work such wonders without formidable powers. It must know how to soar on clouds and ride the mist, and how to pass in and out of the hidden realms. The ancients said it well: ‘Trust not even the seemingly upright; beware the heartless man.’ My lord, do not take offense at our words. If you can capture it, you will rid our remote mountain of this root of calamity, and we shall indeed be blessed by the fortune of three lifetimes; but if you fail to capture it, many grave inconveniences will follow.” Pilgrim said, “What do you mean by ‘many grave inconveniences’?” The monks replied, “To tell you the truth, my lord, though there are around a hundred monks on this remote mountain, every one of us entered the religious life in childhood. When our hair grows, we find a knife to shave it; when our clothes wear thin, we patch our tattered robes. At dawn we rise and wash our faces, then fold our hands, bow low, and take refuge in the Great Way; at night we put things in order, burn incense, devoutly click our teeth, and invoke Amitabha. Raising our heads, we behold the nine grades of the Buddha’s lotus throne, practise the Three Vehicles, and share the compassionate vessel and Dharma-cloud, longing to behold the World-Honored Shakyamuni in the Jeta Grove; lowering our heads, we examine the mind, receive the Five Precepts, and seek to deliver the great chiliocosm, praying through life after life and amid all phenomena to awaken to the emptiness of stubborn delusion and the emptiness of form. When patrons come, old and young, tall and short, stout and thin, we each strike the wooden fish and sound the metal chime, crowding close together as we recite two scrolls of the Lotus Sutra and one volume of Emperor Liang’s Repentance; when no patrons come, whether our robes are new or old, whether we are novices or veterans, rustic or refined, we each join our palms and close our eyes, sitting silently and dimly absorbed upon our meditation cushions, with the moonlit gate firmly barred. We leave the orioles’ cries and birds’ chatter to contend idly among themselves; none can disturb us from the Great Vehicle of skillful compassion. Consequently, we know neither how to subdue tigers nor how to conquer dragons; we cannot recognize a monster, nor can we identify a fiend. If you provoke that demon, my lord, our hundred monks will provide it with no more than one full meal. First, all of us living beings will fall into the cycle of rebirth; second, this ancient Chan monastery will be obliterated; and third, the assembly of the Tathagata will lose every last trace of glory. Those are the many grave inconveniences we mean.”

p.src: When Pilgrim heard the monks speak in this fashion, anger rose in his heart and fury sprang from his gall. He shouted, “What fools you monks are! You know all about that fiend, yet know nothing of what Old Sun can do?” The monks answered softly, “Truly, we do not.” Pilgrim said, “Today I shall briefly tell you. Listen well. On the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit I subdued tigers and conquered dragons; in Heaven itself I raised havoc in the Celestial Palace. When hungry, I took Lord Lao’s elixir and casually chewed two or three pellets; when thirsty, I took the Jade Emperor’s wine and lightly drained six or seven cups. When I open my pair of neither-white-nor-black golden pupils, Heaven turns bleak and the moon grows dim; when I wield my neither-short-nor-long gold-banded cudgel, I come without shadow and depart without trace. What matter whether they are great fiends or petty monsters, no matter how foul and slothful they may be? Once I chase them down, some flee, some tremble, some hide, and some panic; once I seize them, some are hacked, some burned, some ground, and some pounded. Just as the Eight Immortals crossed the sea, each displaying his own divine powers, I alone display mine. You monks, I shall capture this fiend and show it to you; only then will you know Old Sun.”

p.src: As the monks listened, they nodded secretly and thought, “This thieving baldhead opens his mouth wide and boasts extravagantly; perhaps he truly has some notable history.” One after another, they murmured their assent. Only the lama monk said, “Wait. Your venerable master is ill; capturing this fiend is not the most pressing matter. As the common saying goes, ‘When a gentleman attends a feast, if he is not drunk, he will at least be full; when a brave man enters battle, if he does not die, he will at least be wounded.’ If, while the two of you contend, your master should be dragged into the trouble, that would hardly be safe or prudent.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “That is reasonable, quite reasonable. I shall first take cool water to Master, then return.” He lifted the alms bowl, filled it with cool water, left the monastery kitchen, and went straight to the abbot’s quarters, calling, “Master, here is cool water to drink.” Tripitaka was tormented by thirst just then, so he raised his head, cupped the water in his hands, and drank it in a single draught. Truly: When one thirsts, a single drop is sweet dew; when the right medicine arrives, the illness is cured. Seeing that the elder’s spirits were gradually reviving and his brow and eyes relaxing, Pilgrim asked, “Master, could you eat some broth and rice?” Tripitaka said, “That cool water was just like a miraculous elixir. My illness has diminished by half, so I could eat a little broth and rice.” Pilgrim repeatedly called out in a loud voice, “My master is better! He wants broth and rice!” He had the monks hurry to prepare food: they washed rice and cooked it, kneaded dough and baked cakes, steamed buns, and made noodle soup, bringing out four or five tables of dishes. The Tang Monk managed only half a bowl of rice gruel; Pilgrim and Sha Monk consumed just one table, while Bajie packed all the rest into his belly. The utensils were cleared away, lamps were lit, and the monks dispersed.

The utensils were cleared away, lamps were lit, and the monks dispersed.

p.src: Tripitaka asked, “How many days have we been staying here now?” Pilgrim replied, “Three full days. By tomorrow evening, it will be four whole days.” Tripitaka said, “Those three days have cost us a great deal of our journey.” Pilgrim said, “Master, it does not amount to much delay. Let us leave tomorrow.” Tripitaka said, “Quite right. Even if I must travel while still somewhat ill, it cannot be helped.” Pilgrim said, “Since we are leaving tomorrow, let me catch the fiend tonight and see what it is.” Startled, Tripitaka asked, “What fiend are you going to catch now?” Pilgrim replied, “There is a fiend in this monastery. Let old Sun catch it for them.” The Tang Monk said, “Disciple, I am still sick and helpless. Why have you conceived such an idea again? If the creature has supernatural powers and you cannot subdue it, will that not bring harm upon me again?” Pilgrim said, “You truly know how to dampen a man’s courage. Old Sun has subdued fiends wherever he has gone. Whom have you ever seen me prove weaker than? I need only refrain from striking; once I strike, I am certain to win.” Tripitaka caught hold of him and said, “Disciple, the old sayings put it well: ‘When you can oblige another, oblige him; where you can spare someone, spare him.’ ‘How can anxious scheming equal a kindly heart? How can striving to prevail equal the nobility of patience?’” When the Great Sage Sun saw his master earnestly urging him not to subdue the fiend, he told him the truth: “Master, to be perfectly honest with you, that fiend has been eating people here.” The Tang Monk cried in alarm, “Whom has it eaten?” Pilgrim said, “During the three days we have stayed here, it has already eaten six young monks from this monastery.” The elder said, “‘When the hare dies, the fox grieves; creatures mourn for their own kind.’ Since it has eaten monks of this monastery, and I too am a monk, I shall let you go—but you must be most careful.” Pilgrim replied, “Say no more. Once old Sun lays a hand on it, the creature will be done for.”

Stars shone in the sky, but the moon had not yet risen, and the hall was pitch-dark. He breathed out true fire to light the glazed lamps, beat the drum on the eastern side, and struck the bell on the western side. When the sounds had died away, he shook himself and changed into a young monk of only twelve or thirteen, wearing a short yellow-silk robe over a long white habit. p.src: Now that the stars shine and the moon is bright, ours is surely a destined meeting of lovers from a thousand miles apart. Come with me into the rear garden, and there we shall make love and become a mated pair.” Hearing this, Pilgrim nodded to himself and thought, “Those foolish monks were all lured by lust, and that was why they lost their lives. Now she has come to deceive me in the same way.” He readily agreed aloud, saying, “My lady, I am still young and have entered the religious life, so I know nothing of lovemaking.” The woman said, “Come with me, and I will teach you.” Pilgrim laughed inwardly and thought, “Very well, then. I shall go with her and see what she means to do.”

p.src: With arms around each other’s shoulders and hands clasped together, the two left the Buddha hall and went straight to the rear garden. The monster hooked a leg around Pilgrim and tripped him to the ground. Crying “my darling brother” again and again, she reached out to seize his privates. Pilgrim said, “My child, so you truly mean to eat old Sun!” But Pilgrim caught her hand and used a little seated throwing technique to roll the monster over onto the ground. The monster still cried, “My darling brother, how cruelly you throw your lady down!” Pilgrim calculated inwardly, “If I do not strike her now, when will I? As the saying goes, ‘He who strikes first gains the advantage; he who strikes later comes to grief.’” He braced his hands, bent at the waist, and sprang to his feet. Revealing his original form and dharma-image, he swung up his gold-hooped iron staff and struck straight at her head. The monster was indeed taken aback. She thought, “This little monk is remarkably formidable.” Opening her eyes for a closer look, she discovered that it was none other than Elder Tang’s disciple surnamed Sun. Yet she was not afraid of him. And what sort of fiend do you suppose this creature was?

p.src: Trusting in her vast supernatural powers, she instantly raised a pair of swords. With a ringing clang she parried left and blocked right, wheeling east and darting west. Though Pilgrim was somewhat stronger, he could not bring her down. Chill winds rose on every side, and the waning moon lost its light. Just look at the pair of them. What a splendid battle they fought in the rear garden!

p.src: The Great Sage Sun fought in soaring spirits, and his staff never missed its mark by the slightest degree. Realizing that she could not withstand him, the fiend suddenly knitted her brows as a scheme entered her mind, then turned and fled. Pilgrim shouted, “Wretch, where do you think you are going? Surrender at once!” The fiend ignored him and kept retreating. When Pilgrim’s pursuit grew pressing, she slipped the embroidered shoe from her left foot, breathed an immortal breath upon it, recited a spell, and cried, “Change!” It changed into her own likeness and came dancing at him with the two swords, while her true body flickered and transformed into a clear breeze that swept away. Was she not indeed the baleful star fated to bring disaster upon Tripitaka? She rushed straight into the abbot’s quarters, seized Tang Tripitaka, and carried him up into the clouds. Through dim and boundless darkness, in the blink of an eye, she reached Mount Hollow, entered the Bottomless Cave, and ordered her underlings to prepare a vegetarian wedding feast. Of this we shall speak no more for now.

p.src: Now Sun Wukong, growing vexed and irritable from the fight, seized an opening and knocked the demon down with one blow of his cudgel—only to find that it was an embroidered shoe. Wukong realized that he had fallen for her trick and hastily turned to look for his master, but there was no master to be seen. He saw only the Idiot and Sha Monk mumbling something inarticulately. His breast filled with rage, Wukong cared nothing for right or wrong; he raised his cudgel and struck out wildly, crying again and again, “I’ll beat you to death! I’ll beat you to death!” The Idiot panicked, with nowhere to flee. Sha Monk, however, had once been a great general of the Numinous Mountain and was well versed in such situations. Speaking gently and humbly, he came forward, knelt, and said, “Elder Brother, I understand. I suppose you mean to kill the two of us, abandon the rescue of Master, and go straight home.” Wukong said, “Once I have killed you two, I shall rescue him myself.” Sha Monk laughed and said, “What are you saying, Elder Brother? Without the two of us, truly, ‘a single strand cannot make a thread, and one hand alone cannot clap.’ Brother, who will look after the luggage and the horse? Better emulate Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya, who divided gold as friends, than Sun Bin and Pang Juan, who matched wits as enemies. As the old saying goes, ‘To fight a tiger, one still needs one’s own brothers; on the battlefield, none are better than father and sons.’ I beg you to spare us your blows for now. At daybreak we shall join hearts and strength with you and go seek our master.” Though Wukong possessed vast divine powers, he also understood reason and knew how to judge the moment. Seeing Sha Monk plead so earnestly, he relented and said, “Bajie, Sha Monk, get up, both of you. Tomorrow we shall search for Master. But you must exert yourselves.” Hearing that he had been spared, the Idiot was so delighted he would gladly have promised away half the heavens. He said, “Brother, leave all of that to Old Pig!” The brothers brooded and pondered, unable to sleep; they longed to nod the Fusang sun into the sky and blow away all the stars with a single breath.

p.src: The three disciples sat until dawn. As they made ready to leave, the monks of the temple came early to bar the gate and ask, “Where are you going, venerable sirs?” Wukong laughed and said, “It is embarrassing to tell. Yesterday I boasted before everyone that I would catch the demon for you. Not only have I failed to catch it, but I have even lost my master. We are going to look for him.” The monks said in alarm, “Venerable sirs, our paltry affair has instead brought trouble upon your master. But where will you go to find him?” Wukong said, “I know where to look for him.” The monks hurriedly said, “If you are going, there is still no need to rush. Have some morning food first.” They promptly brought out two or three basins of rice in broth. Bajie ate with all his might and cleaned every dish, then said, “Good monks, once we have found Master, we shall come back here for another visit.” Wukong said, “You still mean to come back here and eat their food? Go to the Hall of the Heavenly Kings and see whether that woman is still there.” The monks said, “Venerable sir, she is gone, she is gone. She stayed here that one night, but by the following day she had disappeared.”

p.src: Wukong cheerfully took leave of the monks, told Bajie and Sha Monk to lead the horse and shoulder the luggage, and headed straight back east. Bajie said, “Brother, you have made a mistake. Why are we heading east again?” Wukong said, “What would you know? That woman we tied up in the Black Pine Forest the day before yesterday—I, Old Sun, saw through her completely with my Fiery Eyes and Golden Pupils, while all of you took her for a good person. She is the one who devoured the monk today, and she is also the one who abducted Master. What a fine lady bodhisattva you rescued! Since she has now carried Master off, we must go back along the old road to look for him.” The two exclaimed admiringly, “Excellent, excellent, excellent! You truly have subtlety beneath your rough exterior. Let us go, let us go!”

p.src: Growing anxious, Wukong drew his cudgel, shook himself, and assumed the original form in which he had wreaked havoc in Heaven: three heads and six arms. His six hands wielded three cudgels, with which he thrashed wildly through the forest in a tremendous clatter. Seeing this, Bajie said, “Sha Monk, Elder Brother has flown into a rage. He cannot find Master and has worked himself into a fit of madness.” As it happened, Wukong’s battering along the way drove out two old men: one was the mountain god and the other the local earth god. They came forward, knelt, and said, “Great Sage, the mountain god and earth god have come to pay their respects.” Bajie said, “What miraculous roots! He beats along one stretch and drives out a mountain god and an earth god. If he beats along another, he may even drive out the God of the Year!” Wukong demanded, “Mountain god and earth god, how dare you behave so lawlessly and make common cause with bandits here? When the bandits succeed in their raids, they buy pigs and sheep to sacrifice to you; and you have also colluded with a demon, joining together to abduct my master. Where have you hidden him now? Tell me the whole truth at once, and you will escape a beating.” The two gods panicked and said, “Great Sage, you have accused us unjustly. The demon does not dwell on this humble god’s mountain and is not subject to our jurisdiction. We know only a little from the sound of the wind at night.” Wukong said, “If you know, tell me every detail.” The earth god said, “The demon carried your master due south, to a place a thousand li from here. In that region stands a mountain called Mount Sky-Piercing. Within the mountain is a cave called the Bottomless Cave. It was the demon from that mountain who came here in disguise and carried him away.” Hearing this, Wukong was secretly alarmed. He shouted the mountain god and earth god away, dismissed his magical form, and resumed his usual appearance. Then he said to Bajie and Sha Monk, “Master has been taken far away.” Bajie said, “If it is far, we shall ride the clouds and catch up.”

p.src: Bajie said, “Brother, this mountain is so steep and perilous that there must be some evil spirit here.” Wukong said, “That goes without saying. Where there are lofty mountains, there are always monsters; how could steep ridges be without spirits?” Then he called, “Sha Monk, you and I shall remain here for now. Let Bajie descend into the valley first and make inquiries. He must find out which road is passable, whether there truly is a cave dwelling, and where its entrance lies. Have him investigate everything carefully, so that we can all go together to find and rescue Master.” Bajie said, “Old Pig has rotten luck—you always make me bear the brunt first.” Wukong said, “Last night you said you would take care of everything. Why are you backing out now?” Bajie said, “Stop shouting. I’ll go.” The Idiot set down his rake, shook out his clothes, and, empty-handed, leapt down the high mountain to search for a path.
